title: Find Drivers with Improved Fuel Efficiency
statement:
A fleet logs its drivers and their trips over one calendar year:

- `drivers(driver_id, driver_name)`: one row per driver; `driver_id` is unique.
- `trips(trip_id, driver_id, trip_date, distance_km, fuel_consumed)`: one row per trip; `trip_id` is unique, and `distance_km` and `fuel_consumed` are positive.

A trip's fuel efficiency is `distance_km / fuel_consumed`. Trips from January to June form the first half of the year, trips from July to December the second half. For each driver, `first_half_avg` and `second_half_avg` are the averages of the per-trip efficiencies in each half, and `efficiency_improvement` is `second_half_avg - first_half_avg`.

Report the drivers who have trips in **both** halves and whose second-half average is strictly higher than their first-half average. Output `driver_id`, `driver_name`, `first_half_avg`, `second_half_avg` and `efficiency_improvement`, each average and the improvement rounded to 2 decimals (the improvement is computed from the unrounded averages). Order by `efficiency_improvement` descending, then by `driver_name` ascending.
constraints: All trip dates fall in the same calendar year
Driver names are unique, ignoring letter case
reference:
WITH halves AS (
  SELECT driver_id,
         AVG(CASE WHEN MONTH(trip_date) <= 6 THEN distance_km / fuel_consumed END) AS first_half,
         AVG(CASE WHEN MONTH(trip_date) >= 7 THEN distance_km / fuel_consumed END) AS second_half
  FROM trips
  GROUP BY driver_id
)
SELECT d.driver_id, d.driver_name,
       ROUND(h.first_half, 2) AS first_half_avg,
       ROUND(h.second_half, 2) AS second_half_avg,
       ROUND(h.second_half - h.first_half, 2) AS efficiency_improvement
FROM halves AS h
JOIN drivers AS d
  ON d.driver_id = h.driver_id
WHERE h.second_half > h.first_half
ORDER BY efficiency_improvement DESC, d.driver_name;
brute:
SELECT d.driver_id, d.driver_name,
       ROUND(early.efficiency, 2) AS first_half_avg,
       ROUND(late.efficiency, 2) AS second_half_avg,
       ROUND(late.efficiency - early.efficiency, 2) AS efficiency_improvement
FROM drivers AS d,
     (SELECT driver_id, AVG(distance_km / fuel_consumed) AS efficiency
      FROM trips
      WHERE MONTH(trip_date) BETWEEN 1 AND 6
      GROUP BY driver_id) AS early,
     (SELECT driver_id, AVG(distance_km / fuel_consumed) AS efficiency
      FROM trips
      WHERE MONTH(trip_date) BETWEEN 7 AND 12
      GROUP BY driver_id) AS late
WHERE early.driver_id = d.driver_id
  AND late.driver_id = d.driver_id
  AND late.efficiency > early.efficiency
ORDER BY 5 DESC, 2
notes:
## Intuition

Each driver needs two numbers: the average trip efficiency in January to June and in July to December. Both come from one pass over `trips` with **conditional aggregation**: `AVG(CASE WHEN month <= 6 THEN efficiency END)` averages only first-half trips, because `CASE` yields `null` for the rest and `AVG` skips nulls. A driver with no trips in a half gets a `null` average there, so a single comparison `second_half > first_half` both demands trips in each half and keeps only improvements.

## Approach

1. `halves`: group `trips` by `driver_id`; `first_half` is the average of `distance_km / fuel_consumed` over trips with `MONTH(trip_date) <= 6`, `second_half` over months 7 to 12.
2. Join `halves` (`h`) to `drivers` (`d`) for the name.
3. Keep rows with `h.second_half > h.first_half` (false when either is `null`).
4. Round both averages and their unrounded difference to 2 decimals, then order by `efficiency_improvement` descending and `driver_name`.

## Example 1, step by step

| driver | first-half efficiencies | first_half | second-half efficiencies | second_half | kept |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alice | 11.814, 12.121 | 11.967 | 13.636, 14.400 | 14.018 | 2.05 |
| Bob | 11.111, 11.364 | 11.237 | 13.333 | 13.333 | 2.10 |
| Carol | 9.412, 9.783 | 9.597 | none | null | no |
| David | none | null | 12.500, 12.727 | 12.614 | no |
| Emma | 9.565 | 9.565 | none | null | no |

Bob's improvement is 13.333 - 11.237 = 2.096, which rounds to 2.10; subtracting the rounded averages (13.33 - 11.24) would give 2.09.

## Complexity

- Time: O(T) to scan and group T trips, O(D) for the join with D drivers, and O(K log K) to sort the K results.
- Space: O(D) for `halves`.

## Pitfalls

- Dividing total distance by total fuel: the problem averages per-trip efficiencies, which differ when trips use different amounts of fuel.
- Subtracting the rounded averages instead of rounding the exact difference.
- Forgetting the improvement filter: drivers who got worse (or stayed equal) are not reported.
- Splitting halves at the wrong month: June belongs to the first half, July to the second.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `halves` | one row per driver with `first_half` and `second_half` averages |
| `h`, `d` | a `halves` row and the matching `drivers` row |
| `efficiency_improvement` | the rounded `second_half - first_half` |

narration.1: The halves stage computes each driver's two half-year averages in a single pass over trips.
narration.3: CASE keeps a trip's efficiency only for January to June; AVG ignores the nulls it leaves for other months.
narration.4: The same trick averages the July to December trips.
narration.6: Grouping by driver gives one pair of averages per driver.
narration.11: The improvement is rounded after subtracting the exact averages.
narration.13: The join adds each driver's name.
narration.15: Only drivers with both halves and a strictly better second half pass; a null average fails the comparison.
narration.16: Largest improvement first, and equal improvements in name order.
